Research notes · structured pruning × neuroevolution

Prune and Regrow

Find the parts of a trained network that carry little information, then swap each one for a tiny subnetwork grown from a single node. Here is what the literature already covers, what looks new, how to measure “importance” from inputs, and a working toy run.

Short answer

  • Each piece exists on its own. Scoring neurons by entropy or by their effect on the output, clustering neurons into modules, replacing a block of a trained network with a cheaper one, and growing networks from one unit are all published.
  • The combination looks new. I did not find a paper that picks a low-information region of a trained network and replaces it with a NEAT-style topology grown to imitate that region. The closest are BlockSwap (swap blocks for cheaper fixed designs) and block-wise distillation NAS (search a replacement per block). Neither grows the replacement from nothing. Absence of evidence is not proof; this was a careful but not exhaustive search.
  • The key change I'd make: split “importance” from “replaceability”. A part that barely affects the output should just be deleted or frozen to a constant. Growing a small network pays off for parts that do matter but compute something simple.
  • Tested against classic pruning, the improved version wins at small sizes. The first NEAT version lost by about 2 points. NEAT-merge, where one grown neuron replaces several old ones and the neurons that stay are re-fitted to take over their work, keeps 96.5% accuracy at about 460 parameters, where deleting small weights keeps 85.6%. Most of that gain comes from the re-fitting; growing new neurons helps most at the very smallest size. Letting NEAT add new hidden layers did not shrink it further. Details and the 3D replay are below.
  • Your instinct about inputs is right. Score parts by what happens to the output when you perturb them over many inputs. Training-history signals exist (and work), but they describe the path the optimizer took, not what the finished network uses.

Same budget of fine-tuning for every method

Classic pruning vs NEAT-merge

Each method starts from the same trained network (3,466 parameters, 97.7% test accuracy on average) and runs 6 rounds, each a cut followed by 20 epochs of fine-tuning. NEAT-merge is cut to the same parameter counts that deleting small weights reaches in each round. Bars show the range over 3 seeds.

NEAT-merge criterion, in one line: make the change that loses the least per parameter saved, measured after the neurons that stay are re-fitted to cover for the ones that left.

The changes it can choose from: merge several old neurons into one new neuron, which starts from a single link and adds links one at a time while each helps (NEAT's add-connection); delete one neuron, old or newly grown; or trim the weakest 10% of links in a layer. After each change, the next layer's weights from the surviving neurons are re-solved by least squares so it still receives almost the same signal. That is what turns the survivors yellow: they take over the removed neurons' work. Before choosing, the 6 best-scoring changes each get one epoch of training, and the best one after that wins.

Result: NEAT-merge beats both classic methods once the network is small. At about 459 parameters it keeps 96.5%, where deleting small weights keeps 85.6%. At about 163 parameters it keeps 91.0% against 49.0%. Deleting weak neurons cannot get that small: it ends at 717 parameters and 93.6%. Above about 1,000 parameters all methods are within a point of each other.

What really drives the gain is the re-fitting. The same search without new neurons (“no new neurons” in the table below) is about as good down to about 290 parameters. New neurons pay off at the smallest size: 91.0% against 87.5% at about 160 parameters. In the recorded run, no original neuron was simply deleted. 56 of the 64 were merged into NEAT-grown neurons, many of those were later replaced again by sparser ones, and 6 grown neurons were deleted outright when they stopped earning their place. The final network has 17 hidden neurons, 9 of them grown. The median importance of the neurons that remain rose from 0.0009 to 0.43 (deleting weak neurons ends at 0.19), so what is left is clearly more yellow. In the first NEAT version it ended at 0.0087.

NEAT-deep: letting it add new layers did not shrink it further. Here a new neuron may also start a new hidden layer right behind the neurons it replaces, and links may skip layers as in NEAT. It does use this: in the recorded run 26 of the 73 grown neurons went into new layers, the final network has 5 hidden layers, and 65 of its 135 links skip a layer. But at about 160 parameters it keeps 90.7%, against 90.3% for the same code with new layers and skip links switched off, and the seed ranges overlap (90.0–91.3% against 89.3–91.1%). Differences under about a point are noise here: that switched-off run is the same search as NEAT-merge, yet it lands 0.9 points lower at about 460 parameters just from different tie-breaks. My guess is that on this small digits task the limit is how many pixel links the network keeps, not how deep it is.

The method, step by step

  1. Record activations. Run a few thousand representative inputs (a calibration set) through the trained network and store every hidden activation. Everything below uses only these recordings plus gradients.
  2. Find clusters. Group neurons whose activations rise and fall together across inputs (correlation or mutual information), restricted to neurons that are wired to each other. A useful cluster has a clean boundary: a set of incoming activations and a set of outgoing ones. That boundary is what the replacement must reproduce.
  3. Score each cluster twice. Importance: how much the output changes when the cluster is frozen to its average. Replaceability: how well a very simple function of the cluster's inputs predicts its outputs. Formulas below.
  4. Climb a replacement ladder. For each cluster try, cheapest first: delete it, freeze it to a constant, a low-rank linear map, then a grown network. Stop at the first rung that keeps the output within tolerance.
  5. Grow the replacement. Only for clusters that reach the last rung. Start from a single node, add nodes and connections NEAT-style, and train weights by backprop. The target is local (map the boundary inputs to the boundary outputs), so this is a small regression problem with unlimited free data. That removes most of what makes NEAT slow and prone to stalling.
  6. Stitch and fine-tune. Insert the replacement, fine-tune the whole network briefly so downstream layers absorb small errors, then rescore and repeat.

Measuring importance from inputs

Let aC(x) be the activations of cluster C on input x, āC their average over the calibration set, and p(y|x) the network's output distribution.

Importance: ablation effect on the output

I(C) = E_x [ KL( p(y|x) || p(y|x, a_C ← ā_C) ) ]

Freeze the cluster to its mean (not to zero, which shifts everything downstream) and measure how far the output distribution moves, averaged over inputs. This is the ground truth the cheaper scores try to approximate. It costs one forward pass per cluster over the calibration set, which is fine for hundreds of clusters.

Cheap first-order version

Î(C) ≈ E_x | Σ_j (a_j(x) − ā_j) · ∂L/∂a_j(x) |

One backward pass scores every neuron at once. It is the input-driven Taylor criterion of Molchanov et al. 2019, with the mean instead of zero as the reference. Notice it multiplies two things you mentioned: how much a part varies (a − ā) and how much the output listens to it (the gradient).

Why entropy alone is not enough

Activation entropy or variance measures only the first factor. A neuron can swing wildly while the next layer ignores it, and a quiet neuron can sit on a decision boundary. In the toy run below, entropy ranks neurons only loosely like the true ablation effect (rank correlation ), variance slightly better (), and deviation times outgoing weight best (). Use entropy as a quick filter for dead or near-constant units; it finds those perfectly.

The information-theoretic version of your idea is mutual information between a cluster and the output, I(a_C ; y), as in MINT and the variational information bottleneck approach. It is principled but hard to estimate in high dimensions; the ablation KL is a practical stand-in. Neuron Shapley handles interactions between neurons (two that only matter together) at much higher cost.

Replaceability: the score your idea really needs

R_k(C) = E_x || a_C(x) − f_k(a_in(x)) ||² for the best f_k with k parameters

Fit the ladder of simple functions f_k from the cluster's inputs to its outputs and see how small k can go before the error (or the downstream KL) passes your tolerance. A cluster that is important but has a small k is the ideal target for a grown replacement.

About the training-history idea

It has real precedent: movement pruning keeps weights that moved away from zero during fine-tuning, and synaptic intelligence accumulates each weight's contribution to the loss drop along the training path. They are cheap if you log during training. The drawback is the one you named: they reward what mattered on the way, which can differ from what the final network relies on, and you need the training run. For an already-trained network you didn't log, input-driven scores are the only option anyway.

Replacement ladder

Swapping one cluster

The target is the cluster of neurons in hidden layer 2 (outlined in the Clusters view) with the smallest effect per neuron, excluding dead neurons. The original cluster has parameters. Each surrogate was fitted to reproduce its outputs from layer 1, then inserted with no fine-tuning.

The grown nets are a simplified constructive version of the idea: start empty, add one hidden unit at a time wired to 8 inputs, keep the best of 20 random candidates. A single grown unit (21 parameters) recovers almost all of what freezing loses, which a rank-1 or rank-2 linear map does not. This is one seed on a toy problem, so read it as a sanity check, not a result.

What already exists

Piece of your ideaStatusClosest work
Grow a network from minimal structure (NEAT)DoneNEAT (Stanley & Miikkulainen 2002); successors reviewed in Papavasileiou et al. 2021; deep variants in CoDeepNEAT.
NEAT topology with backprop-trained weights (fixes slow, stalling training)DoneBackprop NEAT (Ha 2016); PropNEAT (2024, GPU-friendly).
Grow one unit at a time, freeze, repeatDoneCascade-Correlation (Fahlman & Lebiere 1989); gradient-guided growth: GradMax, Firefly, Net2Net; grow then prune: GNAP (2026).
Score neurons by effect on loss/outputDoneOptimal Brain Damage (1989); Taylor importance (2019); pruning by explaining (LRP); Neuron Shapley; activation-aware Wanda for LLMs.
Score by entropy / informationDoneEntropy-based channel pruning (Luo & Wu 2017); APoZ (dead-ness); HRank (low-rank feature maps); MINT; NEPENTHE (entropy to remove whole layers).
Score from training historyDoneMovement pruning; Synaptic Intelligence; Lottery tickets (rewind to early weights).
Find clusters/modules of neuronsDoneDetecting modularity (Hod et al., coactivation clustering); Clusterability (Filan et al., weight-graph clustering). Used for interpretability, not pruning.
Merge redundant neuronsDoneData-free parameter pruning; Neuron Merging.
Replace a block of a trained net with a cheaper onePartlyBlockSwap (Fisher-guided, picks from a fixed menu); DNA (block-wise distillation + NAS); ShortGPT (drop low-influence LLM layers).
Replacement grown NEAT-style, targeted by information score, on arbitrary neuron clustersNot foundEvolutionary pruning like EAPruning evolves which channels to keep, not new topology. Surveys: Cheng et al. 2023, Hoefler et al. 2021.

Where it is likely to break

Your baseline is plain structured pruning plus fine-tuning. At equal parameter count it is strong. The grown replacement has to beat “delete the weakest neurons and fine-tune”, or the extra machinery isn't earning its keep.
Fewer parameters is not faster. NEAT topologies are irregular and sparse; GPUs are fast on dense matrices. Expect smaller models, not lower latency, unless you constrain growth to dense blocks.
Local fit, global error. A replacement that matches its cluster with small error can still shift downstream layers. Train it on local error plus the final-output KL, and fine-tune after stitching.
The calibration set defines “importance”. A cluster that is idle on your test inputs may handle rare cases. Include hard and out-of-distribution examples when scoring.
Clusters must have clean boundaries. In an MLP that is easy. In CNNs think channels; in transformers, attention heads and MLP blocks. Cross-layer clusters are the most interesting and the hardest to cut cleanly.
Dead units are the free win. 7 of 64 neurons in the toy net never fire. They need a constant, not a grown network; don't let them flatter the results.

A first experiment

  1. Train an MLP on MNIST, then a small CNN on CIFAR-10, to full accuracy.
  2. Compute ablation KL and the first-order score per neuron and per cluster on 2,000 images; confirm the cheap score tracks the expensive one.
  3. Run the ladder on every cluster. Use a real NEAT library with backprop weights for the last rung (for example neat-python topology search with PyTorch fitting each candidate).
  4. Plot accuracy against total parameters for each method. The toy version is done above: NEAT-merge beats classic pruning below about 750 parameters. Next, check that it holds on MNIST and a CNN, where a layer has hundreds of neurons and the least-squares re-fit must stay cheap.
